title: Humans are not computationally more sophisticated than other systems in nature

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Humans are not computationally more sophisticated than other systems in nature

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: By the Principle of Computational Equivalence, human brains, turbulent fluids, simple cellular automata and the universe as a whole all achieve the same level of computational sophistication, so humans are not fundamentally special in intelligence or complexity.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So this means that there is in the end no difference between the level of computational sophistication that is achieved by humans and by all sorts of other systems in nature and elsewhere.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Historical Perspectives” (from p. 844), p. 844. Scope: humans, natural systems, simple programs and the universe

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-56: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.28

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specific systems can be shown universal, but that fact does not empirically entail absence of all fundamental differences. The claim's evaluative conclusion depends on identifying sophistication with one chosen formal property.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: One could compare systems under a chosen computational-capability measure, such as universality, but universality is binary and does not operationalize equal sophistication, intelligence, efficiency, memory, or complexity across brains, fluids, automata, and the universe.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Computational sophistication has no agreed cross-system metric.

Exact computational models of brains and the universe are unavailable.

Universal computation does not imply equal efficiency or intelligence.

fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.2
analysis feasibility: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.2
discriminating power: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For simple programs the comparison is a theorem: rule 110 is universal, so it meets the computational ceiling usually assigned to any effective procedure. Brains, turbulence, and the universe are part of the sentence and are not known to be universal on public data. Simulations of turbulence show complex flow, which leaves emulation power undecided.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take universality as the level of sophistication: a system matches the ceiling of effective procedure if it emulates a universal computer under a stated encoding. Rule 110 meets this by proof. The same standard applied to a brain model, a turbulent flow, and a candidate law of physics is not settled by existing data.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar-looking complexity is compatible with failure to emulate a universal computer.

A brain or a fluid could fail to be universal while its behavior looks complex.

Universality is proved for some cellular automata and is open for brains, turbulence, and the universe.
